title: Tenali Raman and the Sleep-Loving Servant
summary: Tenali Raman’s neighbor, a wealthy but frustrated merchant named Jagannath, had a servant named Somappa who was afflicted with incurable laziness. Somappa could fall asleep anyw...
keywords: the tale of the lazy servant
full_text:
Tenali Raman’s neighbor, a wealthy but frustrated merchant named Jagannath, had a servant named Somappa who was afflicted with incurable laziness. Somappa could fall asleep anywhere: leaning against a doorpost, sweeping the courtyard, or holding a horse's reins.
Whenever Jagannath scolded him, Somappa would yawn and say:
'Master, sleep is a sacred divine gift; why should I fight nature?'

Jagannath complained to Tenali: 'I pay him three silver coins a month, but he sleeps eighteen hours a day! If I fire him, his poor mother will starve. How can I make him work?'

Tenali smiled: 'Leave Somappa to me for one week. I will cure his passion for sleep.'

Tenali hired Somappa to work at his house, offering an extraordinary employment contract:
'Somappa, I have heard of your deep dedication to sleep.
In my house, you do not need to sweep, cook, or carry water.
Your only job is to sleep continuously upon this comfortable cot on my front veranda from sunrise to sunset!
For every hour you sleep without moving, I will pay you one silver coin!
However, if you open your eyes, sit up, or take a single step off the cot before the sunset gong, you must pay me a fine of five silver coins!'

Somappa could not believe his good fortune:
'To be paid in silver just for sleeping? This is paradise!'

On the first morning, Somappa lay down upon the soft cot, grinning, and fell asleep.
He slept for three hours. But by noon, his back began to ache from lying flat.
He wanted to stretch, but Tenali sat on a stool beside the cot with a notebook, saying:
'Keep sleeping, Somappa! If you move a toe, you owe me five silver coins!'

By afternoon, Somappa was desperately bored, thirsty, and restless. Outside the veranda, boys were playing games, vendors were shouting interesting wares, and life was bustling.
Somappa wanted to get up, but Tenali ordered:
'Sleep, Somappa! Close your eyes! Sleeping is your royal duty!'
By evening, Somappa felt as though the comfortable cot had become an iron torture rack!

On the second morning, when Tenali called him to the cot, Somappa trembled:
'Master Tenali, please, I beg of you! Do not make me sleep!
Let me sweep the courtyard! Let me carry twenty buckets of water from the river! Let me chop five bundles of firewood!
I never realized that forced idleness is worse than the hardest labor!'

Tenali laughed and released him from the contract.
Somappa returned to Merchant Jagannath’s house as the most energetic, industrious worker in the neighborhood, having learned that purposeful work gives sweetness to rest, while forced indolence is a prison.
moral: Ingenious psychological motivation cures chronic indolence better than angry reprimands.
